1H (Number Theory)

Words: 132 Articles: 5
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 56
1H OurBigBook.com
An odd composite integer n>1 coprime to b is a Fermat pseudoprime to base b if bn−1≡1(modn). A Carmichael number is a composite integer satisfying this congruence for every integer b coprime to n. The Korselt criterion says that a composite n is a Carmichael number exactly when it is squarefree and p−1 divides n−1 for every prime divisor p of n.

i

Words: 48 Articles: 1
1H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 48
i OurBigBook.com
By the Korselt criterion, the prime factors are distinct. There cannot be just one prime factor, since a Carmichael number is composite. If there were exactly two, write n=pq with p<q. Then q−1∣pq−1=p(q−1)+(p−1), so q−1∣p−1, impossible because 0<p−1<q−1. Hence at least three distinct prime factors are necessary.

ii

Words: 28 Articles: 1
1H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 28
ii OurBigBook.com
The prime factorization is 561=3⋅11⋅17, so it is composite and squarefree. Moreover 3−1=2, 11−1=10 and 17−1=16 all divide 560=561−1. The Korselt criterion therefore proves that 561 is a Carmichael number.

The complex Taylor theorem says that an analytic function has the expansion
f(z)=∑m=0∞​m!f(m)(z0​)​(z−z0​)m
(1)
throughout every disk centred at z0​ contained in D. In particular it converges for ∣z−z0​∣<dist(z0​,C∖D), and uniformly on every smaller closed disk. The coefficients are uniquely its derivatives divided by factorials. The convergence radius can be larger if the function extends beyond the boundary of D; the theorem does not say that the given domain determines its exact radius.

ii

Words: 138 Articles: 1
2F OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 138
ii OurBigBook.com
An elementary geometric-series construction suffices, without assuming a general polynomial-approximation theorem. Rotate the square by a multiple of π/2 so that ℜw>1. Put c=−R with R>0. Every point of the square then satisfies ∣z−c∣2≤(R+1)2+1, whereas
∣w−c∣2−[(R+1)2+1]=2R(ℜw−1)+∣w∣2−2>0
(2)
for sufficiently large R. Thus the whole square lies inside a disk centred at c whose radius is less than ∣w−c∣. The other three ways w can lie outside the square are handled by the indicated rotations, after which rotating back preserves polynomial form.
Now expand
z−w1​=−w−c1​1−(z−c)/(w−c)1​=−∑j=0∞​(w−c)j+1(z−c)j​.
(3)
Let ρ=maxz∈K​∣z−c∣/∣w−c∣<1. The tail after degree m is uniformly bounded by ρm+1/[∣w−c∣(1−ρ)], tending to zero. Hence the displayed partial sums are the required uniform polynomial approximations. This is the Taylor series about a carefully chosen distant centre, rather than a potentially inadequate series about 0.

3G (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 380 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 380
3G OurBigBook.com
Suppose a connected subset C⊂F contains distinct points a,b. The distance function x↦∣x−a∣ is 1-Lipschitz, and its image on C is connected and contains 0 and ∣b−a∣. It therefore contains the whole interval between those values. A Lipschitz map cannot increase Hausdorff dimension: taking images of arbitrarily fine covers multiplies their diameter powers by at most a fixed constant. Since a nondegenerate interval has Hausdorff dimension one, dimH​C≥1, contradicting dimH​F<1. Thus every connected subset is a singleton, so F is totally disconnected.
A Möbius transformation pairs two disks when it maps their boundary circles to one another and takes the exterior of the first disk onto the interior of the second. Two pairs of disks with disjoint interiors give the ping-pong lemma construction of a free two-generator group. Tangencies are allowed in the convention suggested by the question; this is often called a Tangent-disk Schottky group, rather than a strictly separated Schottky group.
Here is a concrete configuration that also makes the dimension argument precise. Take A(z)=z+2 and B(z)=z/(iz+1). The first pairs the half-plane disks ℜz<−1 and ℜz>1, which are disks on the sphere tangent at infinity. The second pairs ∣z−i∣<1 and ∣z+i∣<1, tangent at zero; their interiors are also disjoint from the half-plane disks. These pairings give a free discrete Kleinian group by ping-pong lemma, with a nonempty open fundamental region.
Set C=ABA−1B−1. Conjugating the subgroup generated by B,C by M(z)=iz/(2−z) gives matrices
MBM−1=(12​01​),MCM−1=(−3−2​21​).
(4)
The product of the second matrix with the first is (10​21​). These are the standard parabolic generators of the principal level-two modular group, whose ideal-quadrilateral fundamental region tiles the upper half-plane and whose Kleinian limit set is the entire extended real line. Consequently the original group's Kleinian limit set contains the circle ∣z−1∣=1, as well as its image under A, the distinct tangent circle ∣z−3∣=1.
It follows that the limit set has Hausdorff dimension at least one and is not homeomorphic to a circle. Indeed a proper subset of a circle cannot itself be a circle: after deleting a missing point it lies in a line, which cannot contain an embedded circle. A space containing two distinct complete circles thus cannot be homeomorphic to a single circle. This explains why dimension at least one does not force circle topology. The tangent-circle terminology is consistent with the primary discussion of T-Schottky configurations in arxiv.org/pdf/math/0701572 .

4J (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 162 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 162
4J OurBigBook.com
Reliable transmission at rate r means that there is a sequence of binary block codes of lengths n, message counts Mn​ with liminfn−1log2​Mn​≥r, and decoding error probabilities tending to zero. The Shannon second coding theorem identifies the supremum of reliable rates with the channel capacity.
For a binary symmetric channel, the conditional entropy of the output given any input bit is h2​(p)=−plog2​p−(1−p)log2​(1−p). The output entropy is at most one bit and attains one for uniform input, so the maximum mutual information is
C=1−h2​(p)​.
(5)
All rates strictly below C are achievable, and rates above C are not reliable; this states the supremum without claiming achievability of every boundary rate under every convention.
For very small p, the capacity is close to one, with h2​(p)=plog2​(1/p)+p/log2+O(p2). At p=1/2, the output is independent of the input and capacity is zero. For p>1/2, flipping every received bit converts the channel to crossover probability 1−p<1/2; its capacity is unchanged because h2​(p)=h2​(1−p). At p=1 the deterministic bit flip is perfectly reversible.

5I (Statistical Modelling)

Words: 240 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 240
5I OurBigBook.com
The first two commands create vectors of observed successes and corresponding numbers of trials. The next two create the class labels and convert them into an R factor, so the labels are treated categorically. The final command fits a grouped-binomial logistic regression, using the proportions as responses and trial totals as binomial weights, and prints its summary. The model is log[πi​/(1−πi​)]=β0​+βb​1{Si​=b}​, with class a as reference.
The intercept estimates the log odds in class a. Its value corresponds to probability 39/287≈0.1359. The class-b coefficient is the estimated increase in log odds, about 0.4999, so the fitted probability in class b is 35/170≈0.2059 and the estimated odds ratio is e0.4999≈1.6485. The printed standard errors measure uncertainty in these estimated coefficients. The z values are estimate divided by standard error: the intercept tests whether the class-a probability is 1/2, while the class-b z value tests equal class probabilities. The two-sided normal-reference P-value for the latter is about 0.051, so it is just above a conventional 5% threshold; this is a borderline result rather than strong evidence of a class effect.
The residual deviance compares the fitted two-parameter model with the four-probability saturated model. Its value 1.9369 on 4−2=2 residual degrees of freedom is small relative to a χ22​ reference, with approximate tail probability e−1.9369/2≈0.380. There is no evidence of lack of fit by that check. Four Fisher scoring iterations were needed for numerical fitting. These interpretations presume independent binomial counts and the usual large-sample approximations; weights here encode trial counts, not extra independent observations.

i OurBigBook.com
Set s=∣w∣2. The exact Hebbian learning rule gives
τs˙=2w⋅(yx)=2y2≥0.
(6)
Thus the norm never decreases, and increases whenever the output is nonzero. Because learning is slow relative to input fluctuations, its averaged equation is τw˙=Cw, where C=⟨xxT⟩ is the input second-moment matrix. It is a covariance matrix only if the inputs have zero mean. Diagonalizing the positive semidefinite matrix C gives components wj​(t)=wj​(0)eλj​t/τ. Hence weights grow without bound whenever the initial vector has a component in an excited positive-eigenvalue direction. A vector entirely in kerC, or identically zero input, is an important stationary exception.

For the modified Hebbian learning rule,
τs˙=2y2(1−αs2).
(7)
It increases below s∗​=α−1/2 and decreases above s∗​, without crossing that equilibrium. More precisely, for a nonzero initial norm,
s(t)+s∗​s(t)−s∗​​=s(0)+s∗​s(0)−s∗​​exp[−τ4α​​∫0t​y(u)2du].
(8)
Under persistent excitation, meaning the integral tends to infinity, this gives
∣w∣⟶α−1/4​.
(9)
Without persistent excitation the limiting norm need not reach this value; zero weights remain zero. The quartic norm stabilization of Hebbian learning bounds the norm and supplies negative feedback at large amplitudes.

iii OurBigBook.com
Averaging the fast fluctuations in yx=xxTw gives
τw˙=Cw−∣w∣2w,C=⟨xxT⟩.
(10)
Thus a nonzero steady vector satisfies
Cw=λw,λ=∣w∣2​.
(11)
Its direction is an eigenvector of the input second-moment matrix, and its magnitude is the square root of that eigenvalue. The zero vector is also a steady state and satisfies the displayed relation with λ=0. This is an averaged steady state; the microscopic fluctuating update need not vanish at each instant.

c

Words: 126 Articles: 1
6E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 126
c OurBigBook.com
Unmodified Hebbian learning reinforces correlated input and output but has no mechanism limiting synaptic strength. The second rule adds activity-dependent negative feedback and stabilizes the norm at an input-scale-independent value, provided the input keeps exciting the output. The third has a cubic weight penalty independent of the instantaneous output; its equilibrium norm instead depends on the strength of the input second moment.
For the third averaged rule, an equilibrium along eigenvector i has radial linearized eigenvalue −2λi​/τ and transverse eigenvalues (λj​−λi​)/τ. Thus a positive simple largest eigenvalue gives stable equilibria in its two opposite directions, whereas lower eigen-directions are unstable to larger components. With generic initial weights, it learns the dominant correlation direction, linking the rule to principal component analysis. These are idealized normalization and feature-extraction mechanisms, not claims that biological synapses implement these exact equations.

7B OurBigBook.com
The fixed points are (0,0) and (±1,1). The Jacobian matrix is
J(x,y)=(1−y2x​−x−1​).
(12)
At the origin its eigenvalues are 1,−1, so it is a saddle with stable direction the y-axis. At either other fixed point, the characteristic polynomial is λ2+λ+2, giving eigenvalues (−1±i7​)/2. Thus both are stable foci. The nullclines are x=0, y=1 and y=x2. In the right half-plane x grows below y=1 and decreases above it; in the left half-plane these horizontal arrows reverse. Vertically, y increases below y=x2 and decreases above it.
A global argument determines the requested omega-limit sets, rather than guessing from the local phase portrait. For x=0, use the quadratic-logarithmic Lyapunov function for a feedback system
L=x2−1−log(x2)+(y−1)2,L˙=−2(y−1)2.
(13)
Its sublevel sets are compact and bounded away from x=0, so trajectories starting in either half-plane exist for all positive time and stay in such a set. Since L decreases, it tends to a limit, and is constant on the omega-limit set. Every point of that set therefore has y=1. Invariance then requires y˙​=x2−1=0, so only the corresponding focus can occur. Also x(t)=x(0)exp(∫0t​(1−y(s))ds) preserves its sign.
Consequently
ω(2,−1)={(1,1)},ω(x,y)={(0,0)} ⟺ x=0​.
(14)
On x=0, the exact solution is y(t)=y(0)e−t. The phase portrait below shows this stable axis, the nullclines and the spiral attraction in each half-plane.

8A (Further Complex Methods)

Words: 192 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 192
8A OurBigBook.com
At zero an ordinary point requires p,q to be analytic. A regular singular point requires zp and z2q to extend analytically to zero, with at least one of p,q failing to be analytic if “singular” excludes ordinary points.
Put ζ=1/z and v(ζ)=w(1/ζ). Differentiation gives w′=−ζ2v′ and w′′=ζ4v′′+2ζ3v′, so the transformed equation is
v′′+(ζ2​−ζ2p(1/ζ)​)v′+ζ4q(1/ζ)​v=0.
(15)
The point at infinity is ordinary precisely when both transformed coefficients are analytic at ζ=0. Solving these conditions for the original coefficients gives
p(z)=2z−1+z−2P(z−1),q(z)=z−4Q(z−1)​,
(16)
with P,Q analytic near zero; the sign can be absorbed into the arbitrary analytic P.
If the only singular point on the sphere is the regular singularity at zero, then zp(z) and z2q(z) are entire. The condition at infinity makes the first tend to 2 and the second to 0. By Liouville theorem they are respectively the constants 2 and 0. Thus the unique equation is
w′′+z2​w′=0​,
(17)
with general solution w=A+B/z. Zero is genuinely regular singular and infinity is ordinary. If “no other singular points” were restricted to finite points only, the general coefficients would instead be p=P(z)/z and q=Q(z)/z2 with entire P,Q; the preceding question about infinity indicates the spherical interpretation.

A one-dimensional canonical transformation is a locally invertible change of phase-space variables preserving the symplectic two-form: dQ∧dP=dq∧dp. Equivalently it preserves Hamilton equations for the transformed Hamiltonian. Expanding the two-form yields
dQ∧dP=(Qq​Pp​−Qp​Pq​)dq∧dp,
(18)
so
{Q,P}=Qq​Pp​−Qp​Pq​=1​.
(19)
Conversely this Jacobian condition makes the transformation locally invertible and symplectic in two dimensions.

β=2,α=1​.

a OurBigBook.com
The physical Jeans length is the wavelength for which pressure and gravity balance:
λJ​=vs​Gρm​π​​​,kJphys​=vs​4πGρm​​​.
(23)
The physical wavelength of the comoving mode is 2πa/k. Modes with wavelength larger than λJ​ have a gravitationally destabilizing coefficient and can grow; shorter wavelengths are pressure-supported and oscillate, with expansion also damping the motion. A time-dependent background makes the exact growth history depend on the epoch, not just an instantaneous sign. For pressureless matter the Jeans length vanishes.

For an Einstein-de Sitter universe, H=a˙/a=2/(3t). The flat matter-only Friedmann equation H2=8πGρm​/3 gives ρm​=1/(6πGt2). With zero sound speed the perturbation equation is therefore
δ¨k​+3t4​δ˙k​−3t22​δk​=0.
(24)
Substituting ts yields s(s−1)+4s/3−2/3=0, or (3s−2)(s+1)=0. Hence
δk​=Ak​t2/3+Bk​t−1​,
(25)
with growing mode proportional to the scale factor and decaying mode proportional to t−1.

c

Words: 105 Articles: 1
10D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 105
c OurBigBook.com
For subhorizon pressureless matter during radiation domination, expansion is too rapid for significant self-gravitating growth. Neglecting the small matter-gravity term gives δ¨m​+t−1δ˙m​≃0, hence a constant plus a logarithm of time; the exact coupled radiation problem supplies the detailed amplitudes. This is the Mészáros effect. Modes entering the horizon during radiation domination are suppressed relative to modes entering later, while after equality ordinary matter growth resumes.
The matter power spectrum consequently has a turnover near the equality horizon scale keq​∼aeq​Heq​ in units with c=1. Shorter-scale modes retain the radiation-era suppression. This statement concerns cold pressureless matter; baryons coupled to photons also show acoustic effects before recombination.

For the continued-fraction assertion, take the standard Pell equation hypothesis N>0 nonsquare. If (x,y) is a solution with x,y>0, then
​yx​−N​​=y2(x/y+N​)1​<2y21​.
(26)
The convergent criterion for continued fractions therefore makes x/y a convergent to N​. Write its periodic expansion as [a0​;a1​,…,aℓ​​], and index convergents by pj​/qj​ with p0​/q0​=a0​. The norm-one convergents occur at j=kℓ−1 with kℓ even. In particular the fundamental positive solution comes at ℓ−1 if ℓ is even, and at 2ℓ−1 if it is odd. If ε=x1​+y1​N​>1 is this least norm-one unit, all integer solutions are represented by ±εm, m∈Z.
The abelian group law comes from multiplication of the norm-one expressions:
(x0​,y0​)∘(x1​,y1​)=(x0​x1​+Ny0​y1​, x0​y1​+x1​y0​)​.
(27)
Their field norms multiply, so the result remains a solution. Multiplication also proves associativity and commutativity; the identity is (1,0) and the inverse of (x,y) is (x,−y). Cubing gives
(x,y)∘3=(x3+3Nxy2, 3x2y+Ny3)=(4x3−3x, (4x2−1)y)​.
(28)
The last form uses Ny2=x2−1.
For completeness, the assertion about all powers follows by dividing any positive unit by the largest power of ε not exceeding it: the remainder is a norm-one unit in [1,ε), and minimality forces it to be 1. Sign changes and inverses give the remaining solutions. If the phrase “nonsquare integer” includes negative N, real continued fractions do not apply: x2+∣N∣y2=1 has only (±1,0) except for N=−1, when (0,±1) also occur. The same multiplication law still works in those finite groups.

11​=3+111​−3​,11​−31​=211​+3​,(11​+3)/2−31​=11​+3,

after which the process repeats. Thus
11​=[3;3,6​]​.

The first two convergents are 3/1 and 10/3, of field norms −2 and 1 respectively. The even period gives the fundamental solution
x=10,y=3​.

It is also directly the smallest positive solution: for y=1,2, the values 1+11y2 are 12,45, neither square; y=3 gives 100. Cubing by the preceding Pell equation group law gives
(10,3)∘3=(3970,1197)​.

12G OurBigBook.com
For s≥0 and δ>0, define the scale-restricted Hausdorff content at scale δ by
Hδs​(F)=inf{∑j​(diamUj​)s:F⊂⋃j​Uj​, diamUj​≤δ},
(33)
using countable covers. The Hausdorff measure is Hs(F)=limδ↓0​Hδs​(F); the limit exists by monotonicity. A conventional dimension-dependent normalizing constant does not change the Hausdorff dimension
dimH​F=inf{s:Hs(F)=0}=sup{s:Hs(F)=∞}.
(34)
At s=0, a nonempty singleton has contribution one, so the measure counts points.
Let T(K)=⋃i=1k​Si​(K) and c=maxi​ci​<1. For compact nonempty K,L, matching a point of Si​(K) with the image of a nearby point of L gives dH​(TK,TL)≤cdH​(K,L). Choose a sufficiently large closed ball B with every Si​(B)⊂B. The nonempty compact sets Tm(B) are nested, so their intersection I is nonempty and compact. The finite union of similarity images commutes with this decreasing compact intersection: a point lying in all unions has some repeated branch index, and compactness supplies a preimage in all the nested sets. Consequently T(I)=I. If J is another invariant compact set, the contraction estimate gives dH​(I,J)≤cdH​(I,J), hence I=J. This proves existence and uniqueness of the invariant set of a finite similarity iterated function system.

The propositional completeness theorem states that Γ⊨ϕ if and only if Γ⊢ϕ. Soundness follows by checking the axioms against truth valuations and noting that modus ponens rule preserves truth. For completeness, use the deduction theorem for propositional logic: if Γ∪{p}⊢q, then Γ⊢p⇒q. In the usual negation rules this also says that a contradiction from Γ∪{p} proves Γ⊢¬p.
First construct a maximal consistent set extending any consistent set Δ. Enumerate all formulas, possible because the primitive propositions are countable. Starting with Δ0​=Δ, add formula ψn​ at step n if consistency is preserved; otherwise add ¬ψn​. This latter addition is consistent: if both extensions gave contradictions, the deduction theorem for propositional logic would prove both ¬ψn​ and ¬¬ψn​ from Δn​, a contradiction already in Δn​. The union M is consistent because a finite proof uses only finitely many newly added premises. It decides every formula: exactly one of ψ,¬ψ belongs to M. It is deductively closed, since an omitted derivable formula would have its negation in M, contradicting consistency.
Assign a valuation v(p)=1 exactly when the primitive proposition p lies in M. Structural induction proves the maximal consistent set truth lemma v(ψ)=1 if and only if ψ∈M. Negation follows from the decision property. For implication, if ψ⇒χ∈M and ψ∈M, modus ponens rule gives χ∈M. Conversely, if χ∈M, the elementary implication axioms give ψ⇒χ∈M. If ψ∈/M, then ¬ψ∈M, and the usual contradiction rule proves ψ⇒χ. These two alternatives match the truth table. The other connectives, if primitive, are handled by their corresponding rules or defined from negation and implication. Thus every consistent set has a valuation satisfying it.
Now suppose Γ⊢ϕ. If Γ∪{¬ϕ} were inconsistent, the deduction theorem for propositional logic would give Γ⊢¬¬ϕ. Here the third axiom ¬¬ϕ⇒ϕ is essential: it would give Γ⊢ϕ, a contradiction. Hence that extension is consistent and has a satisfying valuation. This valuation satisfies Γ and falsifies ϕ, proving the contrapositive of completeness. In this organization of the proof, the explicit classical double-negation elimination occurs in this last consistency step; the construction and truth lemma use the ordinary negation and contradiction rules, not an unmentioned identification of ¬¬ϕ with ϕ.
The propositional compactness theorem says that a set of formulas is satisfiable exactly when each finite subset is satisfiable. If it were not satisfiable, completeness would make it inconsistent. Its finite contradiction proof uses only a finite subset of premises; soundness makes that subset unsatisfiable. This contradicts the assumed finite satisfiability and proves compactness.

Extremal graph theory asks how many edges a graph can have while avoiding a prescribed subgraph. Define ex(n,H) as the maximum number of edges of an n-vertex simple graph containing no copy of H; copies need not be induced. The extremal graph often reveals the structural reason a forbidden configuration must appear.
A complete proof of Mantel theorem illustrates this principle. In a triangle-free graph, the neighborhoods of the endpoints of any edge are disjoint, so d(u)+d(v)≤n. Summing over edges gives ∑v​d(v)2≤nm, where m is the edge count. By Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,
(2m)2=(∑v​d(v))2≤n∑v​d(v)2≤n2m.
(56)
Thus m≤n2/4 when m>0, and the zero-edge case is immediate. A balanced complete bipartite graph is triangle-free and has ⌊n2/4⌋ edges. Therefore
ex(n,K3​)=⌊n2/4⌋​.
(57)
The proof links a local forbidden triangle to a global degree inequality.
The general Turan theorem states that the balanced complete (r−1)-partite graph Tr−1​(n) maximizes the edge count among Kr​-free graphs. Its leading density is (1−1/(r−1))n2/2. A standard symmetrization explanation is to replace a lower-degree vertex by a twin of a nonadjacent higher-degree vertex: no Kr​ is created and the edge count does not decrease. Iterating at the level of twin classes produces a complete multipartite graph with at most r−1 parts. Moving vertices between parts then balances the part sizes and maximizes the number of cross edges. This provides structural intuition beyond the preceding exact triangle proof.
For any fixed graph H with chromatic number r≥2, the Erdős-Stone theorem is
ex(n,H)=(1−r−11​+o(1))2n2​​.
(58)
The lower bound is the Turan construction: an (r−1)-partite graph cannot contain H. To describe the upper-bound proof, fix an edge-density excess above 1−1/(r−1). Apply a regularity partition with an error parameter much smaller than that excess and a positive density threshold. Delete irregular and low-density pairs; the resulting reduced graph still has density above the Turan threshold, so it contains Kr​. The corresponding r vertex classes form pairwise regular, positive-density pairs. The embedding argument successively chooses vertices with large neighborhoods in every remaining class; regularity discards only a small exceptional set at each choice. With the parameters sufficiently small and n sufficiently large, this embeds a complete r-partite graph with ∣V(H)∣ vertices in each part, and therefore a properly colored copy of H. This explains why chromatic number, rather than the exact shape of H, controls the leading quadratic term.
For example χ(C5​)=3, so forbidding a five-cycle still allows asymptotically n2/4 edges, and exceeding that density by any fixed positive fraction eventually forces a five-cycle. For Kr​ the exact Turan theorem strengthens the asymptotic statement. For bipartite H, the theorem gives only o(n2), leaving an important finer problem: for example Ks,t​-free graphs have upper bounds of order n2−1/s from counting common neighborhoods. Extremal results consequently range from exact finite bounds to asymptotic density thresholds and stability questions about near-extremal structure.

For the literal plus-sign energy, η=−1, the phase-gradient current term has the opposite sign and the field equation contains D−12​. Thus the requested set follows after correcting that one energy sign, not from silently varying inconsistent expressions. This is the gauge-coupling sign in Ginzburg-Landau superconductivity.
Now use the intended convention and write ψ=ns​​eiθ with ns​>0. Dividing D1​ψ=0 by ψ separates real and imaginary parts:
∇ns​​=0,ℏ∇θ=qs​A​.
(137)
Thus ns​ is constant on each connected region. The remaining field equation requires α+βns​=0, so for T<Tc​,
ns​=−α/β>0​.
(138)
The current is j=(qs​ns​/ms​)(ℏ∇θ−qs​A)=0. Taking the curl locally gives B=0, hence also solves the Maxwell equation.
For a closed curve on which the order parameter is nonzero and D1​ψ=0, Stokes' theorem gives
Φ=∮C​A⋅dl=qs​ℏ​∮C​∇θ⋅dl=qs​ℏ​[θ]C​.
(139)
Single-valuedness of ψ permits phase change 2πN, so the flux quantum magnitude is h/∣qs​∣ (for Cooper pairs, h/(2∣e∣)). There is an important geometric qualification: if the entire spanning surface lies in the smooth zero-field superconducting region assumed above, its flux and the total boundary winding are zero. Nonzero quantized flux occurs through a hole or vortex core where those assumptions do not hold over the spanning surface. More generally, without j=0 along the curve, the exact quantized quantity is the fluxoid
∮C​(A+qs2​ns​ms​​j)⋅dl=qs​h​N​.
(140)
Thus fluxoid and flux quantization in a superconductor are related but are not interchangeable without the current condition.

36C (General Relativity)

Words: 269 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 269
36C OurBigBook.com
Birkhoff theorem states that every spherically symmetric vacuum solution of Einstein's equations with zero cosmological constant is locally Schwarzschild, with a constant mass parameter. In particular its exterior vacuum geometry is locally static even if the spherical material source moves. Assuming no exterior matter or outgoing matter radiation, the region outside the collapsing star is vacuum with its conserved total mass M, so the given Schwarzschild metric is appropriate there. Spherical gravitational radiation does not provide an extra time-dependent vacuum degree of freedom. Matter emission would invalidate the vacuum premise.
Use units G=c=1 and signature (−,+,+,+) as in the displayed metric. For a radial timelike geodesic, stationarity gives conserved energy per unit mass E=Ft˙. Proper-time normalization gives
−1=−Ft˙2+Fr˙2​,r˙=−E2−F​
(141)
on the ingoing branch. At the horizon F→0, so r˙→−E, with E>0 for an infaller from the exterior. Hence
Δτ=∫2Mr0​​E2−F(r)​dr​
(142)
is finite near the horizon. If release is from rest at a finite radius, the integrable square-root behavior at the release point also gives finite elapsed proper time. Thus the observer crosses the horizon in finite proper time; the Schwarzschild coordinate singularity is not a physical barrier.
By contrast
drdt​=−FE2−F​E​∼−F1​∼−r−2M2M​,
(143)
so t∼−2Mlog(r−2M)+constant diverges. Schwarzschild time is the limiting proper time of stationary observers at infinity. For actual signals, an outward radial null ray adds a propagation delay involving r∗​=r+2Mlog(r/(2M)−1); signals emitted ever closer to the horizon reach a distant observer ever later and increasingly redshifted. No signal emitted at or inside the event horizon reaches that observer. Thus “seeing crossing only after infinite time” means an asymptotic observational limit, not an eventual finite-time sighting.

37E OurBigBook.com
For an incompressible Newtonian fluid the viscous stress is τij​=2μeij​, where eij​=(ui,j​+uj,i​)/2. Its work converted to heat per unit volume is τij​ui,j​. The antisymmetric part of the velocity gradient has zero contraction with symmetric eij​, so
Φ=2μeij​eij​≥0​.
(144)
For potential flow, ui​=ϕ,i​ and mixed derivatives commute, giving eij​=ϕ,ij​ and Φ=2μ∑i,j​ϕ,ij2​.
Use the given linear wave potential with z increasing downward and θ=kx−ωt. The nonzero strain components are
exx​=ωake−kzsinθ,ezz​=−ωake−kzsinθ,exz​=ezx​=ωake−kzcosθ.
(145)
Their squared contraction is 2ω2a2k2e−2kz, independent of the phase. Thus the time-averaged dissipation density is
Φ=4μω2a2k2e−2kz​.
(146)
Depth integration gives dissipation 2μω2a2k per unit horizontal area, or 4πμω2a2 per wavelength and unit transverse width.
The velocity components are ux​=−ωae−kzcosθ and uz​=ωae−kzsinθ. Hence the depth-integrated mean kinetic energy per wavelength is
K=2ρ​k2π​∫0∞​ω2a2e−2kzdz=2k2πρω2a2​​.
(147)
Equal mean potential and kinetic energies give total energy E=πρω2a2/k2. Dividing the dissipation by that energy yields
E˙=−ρ4μk2​E,E(t)∼E(0)e−4μk2t/ρ​.
(148)
The amplitude decays at half this exponent. The small-viscosity and deep-water assumptions justify evaluating the leading dissipation in the inviscid wave field, extending the depth to infinity and neglecting higher-order amplitude corrections.

38E OurBigBook.com
For inviscid barotropic flow, conservation gives ρt​+∇⋅(ρu)=0 and ρ(ut​+u⋅∇u)=−∇p. Linearizing about uniform rest ρ0​,p0​ gives
ρt′​+ρ0​∇⋅u=0,ρ0​ut​=−∇p′,p′=c02​ρ′,c02​=(dp/dρ)ρ0​​​,
(149)
with the derivative adiabatic for ordinary sound.
Taking curl gives ∂t​(∇×u)=0. Therefore the acoustic velocity is irrotational if the initial vorticity is zero. Uniform rest as the background does not alone forbid a superposed stationary vortical perturbation: for example u=ε(siny,0,0), ρ′=p′=0 solves the linearized equations but has nonzero curl. Thus the printed irrotational conclusion requires the usual restriction to the longitudinal acoustic mode. In that mode set u=∇ϕ and absorb a time-only gauge into ϕ, so p′=−ρ0​ϕt​. Continuity gives
ϕtt​−c02​Δϕ=0​.
(150)
This separates the sound wave from the stationary vorticity mode in linear acoustics.
Define the quadratic acoustic energy density and acoustic energy flux by
e=2ρ0​​∣u∣2+2ρ0​c02​(p′)2​,j=p′u.
(151)
Multiplying momentum by u and the pressure form of continuity by p′/(ρ0​c02​) gives
∂t​e+∇⋅j=0​.
(152)
For any progressive plane wave, not necessarily sinusoidal, let ϕ=F(ξ) with ξ=k⋅x−c0​t. Then u=F′(ξ)k and p′=ρ0​c0​F′(ξ). Its kinetic and compressional energy densities both equal ρ0​(F′)2/2, so
j=c0​ke​.
(153)
The energy is transported at the sound speed in the propagation direction. A superposition of oppositely traveling waves can form a standing wave and need not have this pointwise equality; the statement concerns a single progressive wave.
For a spherical outgoing wave, ϕ=F(r−c0​t)/r. Its radial velocity and pressure are
ur​=rF′​−r2F​,p′=ρ0​c0​rF′​.
(154)
Therefore
eK​=2ρ0​​(rF′​−r2F​)2,eP​=2ρ0​​(rF′​)2​.
(155)
They are generally unequal because of the additional near-field velocity term; their difference is ρ0​[F2/r4−2FF′/r3]/2. They agree only to leading far-field order, or for special profile values. This is the near-field energy imbalance in a spherical acoustic wave.

Solution

Words: 171
a OurBigBook.com
At step k=1,…,n−2, isolate the active column tail a=Ak+1:n,k​. If its subtail is already zero, no reflection is needed. Otherwise choose a Householder reflection H=I−2vvT/(vTv) on the active coordinates such that Ha has only its first component nonzero. A cancellation-resistant choice is v=a+sgn(a1​)∥a∥e1​, with an arbitrary positive sign if a1​=0. Embed H as P=diag(Ik​,H) and replace A by PTAP. Previous reduced columns are untouched, and column k now has no entries below the first subdiagonal.
Similarity by an orthogonal matrix preserves skew symmetry. Consequently an upper-Hessenberg result also has zeros above the first superdiagonal, so it is tridiagonal with zero diagonal and opposite-sign corresponding off-diagonal entries.
For the active skew-symmetric block D, compute w=2Dv/(vTv). Because vTDv=0, expanding the two-sided reflection simplifies to
HDH=D+vwT−wvT​.
(156)
Store and update just one triangle, obtain the other by negation, and keep the diagonal exactly zero. Matrix-vector multiplication can likewise use each stored entry once to contribute to two output coordinates. This is skew-symmetric Householder tridiagonalization; there is no need for two dense matrix-matrix multiplications.

b

Words: 147 Articles: 1
39A OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 147
b OurBigBook.com
Let the active block have size m. Using a stored skew triangle, the product Dv costs m(m−1) scalar multiplications: two for each unordered off-diagonal pair. Updating its stored triangle with vwT−wvT costs another m(m−1) products. Reflector construction, scalings and the active column take only O(m) additional products. Summing over m=n−1,…,2 gives
skew-symmetric cost=32​n3+O(n2) products​.
(157)
For a symmetric block, an optimized matrix-vector calculation costs m2 products, and the symmetric rank-two update of one triangle costs m(m+1) products. The additional scalar vTDv and its correction to the update vector cost only O(m) per step. Thus
symmetric cost=32​n3+O(n2) products​.
(158)
The leading terms are the same under the requested product-count convention. Skew symmetry removes the diagonal work and the scalar correction, giving lower-order savings, not a factor-of-two leading advantage over an already symmetry-aware implementation. Counting additions as well would change the reported flop constants; it is not the convention requested here.
